10: # 1. Overview
11: 
12: The default method by which SQLite implements
13: atomic commit and rollback is a rollback journal .
14: Beginning with version 3.7.0 (2010-07-21), a new "Write-Ahead Log" option
15: (hereafter referred to as "WAL") is available.
16: 
17: There are advantages and disadvantages to using WAL instead of
18: a rollback journal. Advantages include:
19: 
20: WAL is significantly faster in most scenarios.
21: 
22: WAL provides more concurrency as readers do not block writers and
23: a writer does not block readers. Reading and writing can proceed
24: concurrently.
25: 
26: Disk I/O operations tends to be more sequential using WAL.
27: 
28: WAL uses many fewer fsync() operations and is thus less vulnerable to
29: problems on systems where the fsync() system call is broken.
30: 
31: But there are also disadvantages:
32: 
33: All processes using a database must be on the same host computer;
34: WAL does not work over a network filesystem. This is because WAL requires
35: all processes to share a small amount of memory and processes on
36: separate host machines obviously cannot share memory with each other.
37: 
38: Transactions that involve changes against multiple ATTACHed
39: databases are atomic for each individual database, but are not
40: atomic across all databases as a set.
41: 
42: It is not possible to change the page_size after entering WAL
43: mode, either on an empty database or by using VACUUM or by restoring
44: from a backup using the backup API . You must be in a rollback journal
45: mode to change the page size.
46: 
47: It is not possible to open read-only WAL databases .
48: The opening process must have write privileges for " -shm "
49: wal-index shared memory file associated with the database, if that
50: file exists, or else write access on the directory containing
51: the database file if the " -shm " file does not exist.
52: Beginning with version 3.22.0 (2018-01-22), a read-only
53: WAL-mode database file can be opened if
54: the -shm and -wal files
55: already exist or those files can be created or the
56: database is immutable .
57: 
58: WAL might be very slightly slower (perhaps 1% or 2% slower)
59: than the traditional rollback-journal approach
60: in applications that do mostly reads and seldom write.
61: 
62: There is an additional quasi-persistent " -wal " file and
63: " -shm " shared memory file associated with each
64: database, which can make SQLite less appealing for use as an
65: application file-format .
66: 
67: There is the extra operation of checkpointing which, though automatic
68: by default, is still something that application developers need to
69: be mindful of.
70: 
71: WAL works best with smaller transactions. WAL does
72: not work well for very large transactions. For transactions larger than
73: about 100 megabytes, traditional rollback journal modes will likely
74: be faster. For transactions in excess of a gigabyte, WAL mode may
75: fail with an I/O or disk-full error.
76: It is recommended that one of the rollback journal modes be used for
77: transactions larger than a few dozen megabytes.
78: Beginning with version 3.11.0 (2016-02-15),
79: WAL mode works as efficiently with
80: large transactions as does rollback mode.
81: 
82: # 2. How WAL Works
83: 
84: The traditional rollback journal works by writing a copy of the
85: original unchanged database content into a separate rollback journal file
86: and then writing changes directly into the database file. In the
87: event of a crash or ROLLBACK , the original content contained in the
88: rollback journal is played back into the database file to
89: revert the database file to its original state. The COMMIT occurs
90: when the rollback journal is deleted.
91: 
92: The WAL approach inverts this. The original content is preserved
93: in the database file and the changes are appended into a separate
94: WAL file. A COMMIT occurs when a special record indicating a commit
95: is appended to the WAL. Thus a COMMIT can happen without ever writing
96: to the original database, which allows readers to continue operating
97: from the original unaltered database while changes are simultaneously being
98: committed into the WAL. Multiple transactions can be appended to the
99: end of a single WAL file.
100: 
101: ## 2.1. Checkpointing
102: 
103: Of course, one wants to eventually transfer all the transactions that
104: are appended in the WAL file back into the original database. Moving
105: the WAL file transactions back into the database is called a
106: " checkpoint ".
107: 
108: Another way to think about the difference between rollback and
109: write-ahead log is that in the rollback-journal
110: approach, there are two primitive operations, reading and writing,
111: whereas with a write-ahead log
112: there are now three primitive operations: reading, writing, and
113: checkpointing.
114: 
115: By default, SQLite does a checkpoint automatically when the WAL file
116: reaches a threshold size of 1000 pages. (The
117: SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT compile-time option can be used to
118: specify a different default.) Applications using WAL do
119: not have to do anything in order for these checkpoints to occur.
120: But if they want to, applications can adjust the automatic checkpoint
121: threshold. Or they can turn off the automatic checkpoints and run
122: checkpoints during idle moments or in a separate thread or process.
123: 
124: ## 2.2. Concurrency
125: 
126: When a read operation begins on a WAL-mode database, it first
127: remembers the location of the last valid commit record in the WAL.
128: Call this point the "end mark". Because the WAL can be growing and
129: adding new commit records while various readers connect to the database,
130: each reader can potentially have its own end mark. But for any
131: particular reader, the end mark is unchanged for the duration of the
132: transaction, thus ensuring that a single read transaction only sees
133: the database content as it existed at a single point in time.
134: 
135: When a reader needs a page of content, it first checks the WAL to
136: see if that page appears there, and if so it pulls in the last copy
137: of the page that occurs in the WAL prior to the reader's end mark.
138: If no copy of the page exists in the WAL prior to the reader's end mark,
139: then the page is read from the original database file. Readers can
140: exist in separate processes, so to avoid forcing every reader to scan
141: the entire WAL looking for pages (the WAL file can grow to
142: multiple megabytes, depending on how often checkpoints are run), a
143: data structure called the "wal-index" is maintained in shared memory
144: which helps readers locate pages in the WAL quickly and with a minimum
145: of I/O. The wal-index greatly improves the performance of readers,
146: but the use of shared memory means that all readers must exist on the
147: same machine. This is why the write-ahead log implementation will not
148: work on a network filesystem.
149: 
150: Writers merely append new content to the end of the WAL file.
151: Because writers do nothing that would interfere with the actions of
152: readers, writers and readers can run at the same time. However,
153: since there is only one WAL file, there can only be one writer at
154: a time.
155: 
156: A checkpoint operation takes content from the WAL file
157: and transfers it back into the original database file.
158: A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers, however the checkpoint
159: must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark
160: of any current reader. The checkpoint has to stop at that point because
161: otherwise it might overwrite part of the database file that the reader
162: is actively using. The checkpoint remembers (in the wal-index) how far
163: it got and will resume transferring content from the WAL to the database
164: from where it left off on the next invocation.
165: 
166: Thus a long-running read transaction can prevent a checkpointer from
167: making progress. But presumably every read transaction will eventually
168: end and the checkpointer will be able to continue.
169: 
170: Whenever a write operation occurs, the writer checks how much progress
171: the checkpointer has made, and if the entire WAL has been transferred into
172: the database and synced and if no readers are making use of the WAL, then
173: the writer will rewind the WAL back to the beginning and start putting new
174: transactions at the beginning of the WAL. This mechanism prevents a WAL
175: file from growing without bound.
176: 
177: ## 2.3. Performance Considerations
178: 
179: Write transactions are very fast since they only involve writing
180: the content once (versus twice for rollback-journal transactions)
181: and because the writes are all sequential. Further, syncing the
182: content to the disk is not required, as long as the application is
183: willing to sacrifice durability following a power loss or hard reboot.
184: (Writers sync the WAL on every transaction commit if
185: PRAGMA synchronous is set to FULL but omit this sync if
186: PRAGMA synchronous is set to NORMAL.)
187: 
188: On the other hand, read performance deteriorates as the WAL file
189: grows in size since each reader must check the WAL file for the content
190: and the time needed to check the WAL file is proportional
191: to the size of the WAL file. The wal-index helps find content
192: in the WAL file much faster, but performance still falls off with
193: increasing WAL file size. Hence, to maintain good read performance
194: it is important to keep the WAL file size down by
195: running checkpoints at regular intervals.
196: 
197: Checkpointing does require sync operations in order to avoid
198: the possibility of database corruption following a power loss
199: or hard reboot. The WAL must be synced to persistent storage
200: prior to moving content from the WAL into the database and the
201: database file must be synced prior to resetting the WAL.
202: Checkpoint also requires more seeking.
203: The checkpointer makes an effort to
204: do as many sequential page writes to the database as it can (the pages
205: are transferred from WAL to database in ascending order) but even
206: then there will typically be many seek operations interspersed among
207: the page writes. These factors combine to make checkpoints slower than
208: write transactions.
209: 
210: The default strategy is to allow successive write transactions to
211: grow the WAL until the WAL becomes about 1000 pages in size, then to
212: run a checkpoint operation for each subsequent COMMIT until the WAL
213: is reset to be smaller than 1000 pages. By default, the checkpoint will be
214: run automatically by the same thread that does the COMMIT that pushes
215: the WAL over its size limit. This has the effect of causing most
216: COMMIT operations to be very fast but an occasional COMMIT (those that trigger
217: a checkpoint) to be much slower. If that effect is undesirable, then
218: the application can disable automatic checkpointing and run the
219: periodic checkpoints in a separate thread, or separate process.
220: (Links to commands and interfaces to accomplish this are
221: shown below .)
222: 
223: Note that with PRAGMA synchronous set to NORMAL, the checkpoint
224: is the only operation to issue an I/O barrier or sync operation
225: (fsync() on unix or FlushFileBuffers() on windows). If an application
226: therefore runs checkpoint in a separate thread or process, the main
227: thread or process that is doing database queries and updates will never
228: block on a sync operation. This helps to prevent "latch-up" in applications
229: running on a busy disk drive. The downside to
230: this configuration is that transactions are no longer durable and
231: might rollback following a power failure or hard reset.
232: 
233: Notice too that there is a tradeoff between average read performance
234: and average write performance. To maximize the read performance,
235: one wants to keep the WAL as small as possible and hence run checkpoints
236: frequently, perhaps as often as every COMMIT. To maximize
237: write performance, one wants to amortize the cost of each checkpoint
238: over as many writes as possible, meaning that one wants to run checkpoints
239: infrequently and let the WAL grow as large as possible before each
240: checkpoint. The decision of how often to run checkpoints may therefore
241: vary from one application to another depending on the relative read
242: and write performance requirements of the application.
243: The default strategy is to run a checkpoint once the WAL
244: reaches 1000 pages and this strategy seems to work well in test applications on
245: workstations, but other strategies might work better on different
246: platforms or for different workloads.

248: # 3. Activating And Configuring WAL Mode
249: 
250: An SQLite database connection defaults to
251: journal_mode=DELETE . To convert to WAL mode, use the
252: following pragma:
253: 
254: PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;
255: 
256: The journal_mode pragma returns a string which is the new journal mode.
257: On success, the pragma will return the string " wal ". If
258: the conversion to WAL could not be completed (for example, if the VFS
259: does not support the necessary shared-memory primitives) then the
260: journaling mode will be unchanged and the string returned from the
261: primitive will be the prior journaling mode (for example " delete ").
262: 
263: ## 3.1. Automatic Checkpoint
264: 
265: By default, SQLite will automatically checkpoint whenever a COMMIT
266: occurs that causes the WAL file to be 1000 pages or more in size, or when the
267: last database connection on a database file closes. The default
268: configuration is intended to work well for most applications.
269: But programs that want more control can force a checkpoint
270: using the wal_checkpoint pragma or by calling the
271: sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() C interface. The automatic checkpoint
272: threshold can be changed or automatic checkpointing can be completely
273: disabled using the wal_autocheckpoint pragma or by calling the
274: sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint() C interface. A program can also
275: use sqlite3_wal_hook() to register a callback to be invoked whenever
276: any transaction commits to the WAL. This callback can then invoke
277: sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() or sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() based on whatever
278: criteria it thinks is appropriate. (The automatic checkpoint mechanism
279: is implemented as a simple wrapper around sqlite3_wal_hook() .)
280: 
281: ## 3.2. Application-Initiated Checkpoints
282: 
283: An application can initiate a checkpoint using any writable database
284: connection on the database simply by invoking
285: sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() or sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() .
286: There are three subtypes of checkpoints that vary in their aggressiveness:
287: PASSIVE, FULL, and RESTART. The default checkpoint style is PASSIVE, which
288: does as much work as it can without interfering with other database
289: connections, and which might not run to completion if there are
290: concurrent readers or writers.
291: All checkpoints initiated by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() and
292: by the automatic checkpoint mechanism are PASSIVE. FULL and RESTART
293: checkpoints try harder to run the checkpoint to completion and can only
294: be initiated by a call to sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() . See the
295: sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() documentation for additional information
296: on FULL and RESET checkpoints.
297: 
298: ## 3.3. Persistence of WAL mode
299: 
300: Unlike the other journaling modes,
301: PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL is
302: persistent. If a process sets WAL mode, then closes and reopens the
303: database, the database will come back in WAL mode. In contrast, if
304: a process sets (for example) PRAGMA journal_mode=TRUNCATE and then closes and
305: reopens the database will come back up in the default rollback mode of
306: DELETE rather than the previous TRUNCATE setting.
307: 
308: The persistence of WAL mode means that applications can be converted
309: to using SQLite in WAL mode without making any changes to the application
310: itself. One has merely to run " PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL; " on the
311: database file(s) using the command-line shell or other utility, then
312: restart the application.
313: 
314: The WAL journal mode will be set on all
315: connections to the same database file if it is set on any one connection.
316: 
317: # 4. The WAL File
318: 
319: While a database connection is open on a WAL-mode database, SQLite
320: maintains an extra journal file called a "Write Ahead Log" or "WAL File".
321: The name of this file on disk is usually the name of the database file
322: with an extra " -wal " suffix, though different naming rules may
323: apply if SQLite is compiled with SQLITE_ENABLE_8_3_NAMES .
324: 
325: The WAL file exists for as long as any database connection has the
326: database open. Usually, the WAL file is deleted automatically when the
327: last connection to the database closes. However, if the last process to
328: have the database open exits without cleanly
329: shutting down the database connection, or if the
330: SQLITE_FCNTL_PERSIST_WAL file control is used, then the WAL file
331: might be retained on disk after all connections to the database have
332: been closed. The WAL file is part of the persistent state of the
333: database and should be kept with the database if the database is copied
334: or moved. If a database file is separated from its WAL file, then
335: transactions that were previously committed to the database might be lost,
336: or the database file might become corrupted.
337: The only safe way to remove a WAL file is
338: to open the database file using one of the sqlite3_open() interfaces
339: then immediately close the database using sqlite3_close() .
340: 
341: The WAL file format is precisely defined and is cross-platform.
342: 
343: # 5. Read-Only Databases
344: 
345: Older versions of SQLite could not read a WAL-mode database that was
346: read-only. In other words, write access was required in order to read a
347: WAL-mode database. This constraint was relaxed beginning with
348: SQLite version 3.22.0 (2018-01-22).
349: 
350: On newer versions of SQLite,
351: a WAL-mode database on read-only media, or a WAL-mode database that lacks
352: write permission, can still be read as long as one or more of the following
353: conditions are met:
354: 
355: The -shm and -wal files already exist and are readable.
356: 
357: There is write permission on the directory containing the database so
358: that the -shm and -wal files can be created.
359: 
360: The database connection is opened using the
361: immutable query parameter .
362: 
363: Even though it is possible to open a read-only WAL-mode database,
364: it is good practice to convert the database to
365: PRAGMA journal_mode=DELETE prior to burning an
366: SQLite database image onto read-only media.
367: 
368: # 6. Avoiding Excessively Large WAL Files
369: 
370: In normal cases, new content is appended to the WAL file until the
371: WAL file accumulates about 1000 pages (and is thus about 4MB
372: in size) at which point a checkpoint is automatically run and the WAL file
373: is recycled. The checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file
374: (unless the journal_size_limit pragma is set). Instead, it merely
375: causes SQLite to start overwriting the WAL file from the beginning.
376: This is done because it is normally faster to overwrite an existing file
377: than to append. When the last connection to a database closes, that
378: connection does one last checkpoint and then deletes the WAL and its
379: associated shared-memory file, to clean up the disk.
380: 
381: So in the vast majority of cases, applications need not worry about
382: the WAL file at all. SQLite will automatically take care of it. But
383: it is possible to get SQLite into a state where the WAL file will grow
384: without bound, causing excess disk space usage and slow query speeds.
385: The following bullets enumerate some of the ways that this can happen
386: and how to avoid them.
387: 
388: Disabling the automatic checkpoint mechanism.
389: In its default configuration, SQLite will checkpoint the WAL file at the
390: conclusion of any transaction when the WAL file is more than 1000 pages
391: long. However, compile-time and run-time options exist that can disable
392: or defer this automatic checkpoint. If an application disables the
393: automatic checkpoint, then there is nothing to prevent the WAL file
394: from growing excessively.
395: 
396: Checkpoint starvation.
397: A checkpoint is only able to run to completion, and reset the WAL file,
398: if there are no other database connections using the WAL file. If another
399: connection has a read transaction open,
400: then the checkpoint cannot reset the WAL file because
401: doing so might delete content out from under the reader.
402: The checkpoint will do as much work as it can without upsetting the
403: reader, but it cannot run to completion.
404: The checkpoint will start up again where it left off after the next
405: write transaction. This repeats until some checkpoint is able to complete.
406: 
407: However, if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers
408: and there is always at least one active reader, then
409: no checkpoints will be able to complete
410: and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.
411: 
412: This scenario can be avoided by ensuring that there are "reader gaps":
413: times when no processes are reading from the
414: database and that checkpoints are attempted during those times.
415: In applications with many concurrent readers, one might also consider
416: running manual checkpoints with the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART or
417: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE option which will ensure that the checkpoint
418: runs to completion before returning. The disadvantage of using
419: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART and SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE is that
420: readers might block while the checkpoint is running.
421: 
422: Very large write transactions.
423: A checkpoint can only complete when no other transactions are running,
424: which means the WAL file cannot be reset in the middle of a write
425: transaction. So a large change to a large database
426: might result in a large WAL file. The WAL file will be checkpointed
427: once the write transaction completes (assuming there are no other readers
428: blocking it) but in the meantime, the file can grow very big.
429: 
430: As of SQLite version 3.11.0 (2016-02-15),
431: the WAL file for a single transaction
432: should be proportional in size to the transaction itself. Pages that
433: are changed by the transaction should only be written into the WAL file
434: once. However, with older versions of SQLite, the same page might be
435: written into the WAL file multiple times if the transaction grows larger
436: than the page cache.
437: 
438: # 7. Implementation Of Shared-Memory For The WAL-Index
439: 
440: The wal-index is implemented using an ordinary file that is
441: mmapped for robustness. Early (pre-release) implementations of WAL mode
442: stored the wal-index in volatile shared-memory, such as files created in
443: /dev/shm on Linux or /tmp on other unix systems. The problem
444: with that approach is that processes with a different root directory
445: (changed via chroot )
446: will see different files and hence use different shared memory areas,
447: leading to database corruption. Other methods for creating nameless
448: shared memory blocks are not portable across the various flavors of
449: unix. And we could not find any method to create nameless shared
450: memory blocks on windows. The only way we have found to guarantee
451: that all processes accessing the same database file use the same shared
452: memory is to create the shared memory by mmapping a file in the same
453: directory as the database itself.
454: 
455: Using an ordinary disk file to provide shared memory has the
456: disadvantage that it might actually do unnecessary disk I/O by
457: writing the shared memory to disk. However, the developers do not
458: think this is a major concern since the wal-index rarely exceeds
459: 32 KiB in size and is never synced. Furthermore, the wal-index
460: backing file is deleted when the last database connection disconnects,
461: which often prevents any real disk I/O from ever happening.
462: 
463: Specialized applications for which the default implementation of
464: shared memory is unacceptable can devise alternative methods via a
465: custom VFS .
466: For example, if it is known that a particular database
467: will only be accessed by threads within a single process, the wal-index
468: can be implemented using heap memory instead of true shared memory.
469: 
470: # 8. Use of WAL Without Shared-Memory
471: 
472: Beginning in SQLite version 3.7.4 (2010-12-07),
473: WAL databases can be created, read, and
474: written even if shared memory is unavailable as long as the
475: locking_mode is set to EXCLUSIVE before the first attempted access.
476: In other words, a process can interact with
477: a WAL database without using shared memory if that
478: process is guaranteed to be the only process accessing the database.
479: This feature allows WAL databases to be created, read, and written
480: by legacy VFSes that lack the "version 2" shared-memory
481: methods xShmMap, xShmLock, xShmBarrier, and xShmUnmap on the
482: sqlite3_io_methods object.
483: 
484: If EXCLUSIVE locking mode
485: is set prior to the first WAL-mode
486: database access, then SQLite never attempts to call any of the
487: shared-memory methods and hence no shared-memory
488: wal-index is ever created.
489: In that case, the database connection remains in EXCLUSIVE mode
490: as long as the journal mode is WAL; attempts to change the locking
491: mode using " PRAGMA locking_mode=NORMAL; " are no-ops.
492: The only way to change out of EXCLUSIVE locking mode is to first
493: change out of WAL journal mode.
494: 
495: If NORMAL locking mode is in effect for the first WAL-mode database
496: access, then the shared-memory wal-index is created. This means that the
497: underlying VFS must support the "version 2" shared-memory.
498: If the VFS does not support shared-memory methods, then the attempt to
499: open a database that is already in WAL mode, or the attempt to convert a
500: database into WAL mode, will fail.
501: As long as exactly one connection is using a shared-memory wal-index,
502: the locking mode can be changed freely between NORMAL and EXCLUSIVE.
503: It is only when the shared-memory wal-index is omitted, when the locking
504: mode is EXCLUSIVE prior to the first WAL-mode database access, that the
505: locking mode is stuck in EXCLUSIVE.
506: 
507: # 9. Sometimes Queries Return SQLITE_BUSY In WAL Mode
508: 
509: The second advantage of WAL-mode is that
510: writers do not block readers and readers do not block writers.
511: This is mostly true.
512: But there are some obscure cases where a query against a WAL-mode
513: database can return SQLITE_BUSY , so applications should be prepared
514: for that happenstance.
515: 
516: Cases where a query against a WAL-mode database can return SQLITE_BUSY
517: include the following:
518: 
519: If another database connection has the database mode open
520: in exclusive locking mode then all queries against the
521: database will return SQLITE_BUSY . Both Chrome and Firefox open their
522: database files in exclusive locking mode, so attempts to read Chrome or
523: Firefox databases while the applications are running will run into this
524: problem, for example.
525: 
526: When the last connection to a particular database is closing,
527: that connection will acquire an exclusive lock for a short time while
528: it cleans up the WAL and shared-memory files. If a separate attempt
529: is made to open and query the database while the first connection is
530: still in the middle of its cleanup process, the second connection
531: might get an SQLITE_BUSY error.
532: 
533: If the last connection to a database crashed, then the first new
534: connection to open the database will start a recovery process. An
535: exclusive lock is held during recovery. So if a third database connection
536: tries to jump in and query while the second connection is running recovery,
537: the third connection will get an SQLITE_BUSY error.
538: 
539: # 10. Backwards Compatibility
540: 
541: The database file format is unchanged for WAL mode. However, the
542: WAL file and the wal-index are new concepts and so older versions of
543: SQLite will not know
544: how to recover a crashed SQLite database that was operating in WAL mode
545: when the crash occurred.
546: To prevent older versions of SQLite (prior to version 3.7.0, 2010-07-22)
547: from trying to recover
548: a WAL-mode database (and making matters worse) the database file format
549: version numbers (bytes 18 and 19 in the database header )
550: are increased from 1 to 2 in WAL mode.
551: Thus, if an older version of SQLite attempts to connect to an SQLite
552: database that is operating in WAL mode, it will report an error along
553: the lines of "file is encrypted or is not a database".
554: 
555: One can explicitly change out of WAL mode using a pragma such as
556: this:
557: 
558: PRAGMA journal_mode=DELETE;
559: 
560: Deliberately changing out of WAL mode changes the database file format
561: version numbers back to 1 so that older versions of SQLite can once again
562: access the database file.
563: 
564: # 11. The WAL-Reset Bug
565: 
566: On 2026-03-03, one of the SQLite developers (Dan) found and fixed
567: a bug that could, in rare cases, lead to database corruption. We call
568: this the "WAL-reset bug".
569: Key points:
570: 
571: The bug is likely present in all version of SQLite from
572: 3.7.0 (2010-07-21) through 3.51.2 (2026-01-09). It is
573: fixed in version 3.51.3 (2026-03-13) and later. Backports of the fix
574: are available for some earlier releases:
575: 3.44.6 and
576: 3.50.7 .
577: 
578: The bug only affects databases in WAL mode when there are two or more
579: database connections open on the same file, in separate threads or processes,
580: and when those two connections attempt to write or checkpoint at the
581: same instant.
582: 
583: The bug is a data race with tight timing constraints and that requires
584: an unusual usage pattern. It is unlikely
585: to occur in common use. The developers were unable to reproduce
586: the bug organically and had to add special testing logic to SQLite
587: that deliberately triggers the circumstances of the the bug in order
588: to verify that the issue has been fixed.
589: 
590: ## 11.1. Bug Details
591: 
592: This is what happens:
593: 
594: One connection does a checkpoint . This first checkpoint must be
595: complete. In other words, the checkpoint must successfully copy all
596: content from the WAL file back into the database and leave the WAL file
597: in a state where it can potentially be reset.
598: 
599: Shortly after the first checkpoint completes, a second checkpoint
600: is started.
601: 
602: While the second checkpoint from step 2 is starting up, another database
603: connection commits a transaction that resets the WAL file and writes new
604: content into the beginning of the WAL file.
605: 
606: Due to a data race, the second checkpoint from step 2 does not realize
607: that the WAL file has been reset by the transaction commit in step 3.
608: The second checkpoint leaves a field in the header of the WAL-Index set
609: incorrectly. That field indicates that part of the WAL file has already
610: been checkpointed, when in fact it has not been.
611: 
612: Additional transactions are committed to increase the number of pages
613: in the WAL file to be more than were present for the first checkpoint
614: from step 1.
615: 
616: Later when a third checkpoint occurs, the third checkpoint skips all
617: or part of the transaction that was written in step 3. Thus parts of
618: the transaction from step 3 never reach the database file, and the
619: database file goes corrupt.
620: 
621: ## 11.2. Low Probability Of Occurrence
622: 
623: In order for this bug to happen, many details must align at just
624: the right moment. So much so that the SQLite developers were unable
625: to reproduce the bug organically in the lab. The only way the developers
626: have been able to cause the malfunction was to modify the SQLite sources
627: to invoke a callback controlled by sqlite3_test_control()
628: that enables a test program or script to trigger the write transaction
629: of step 3 at just the right moment during the second checkpoint.
630: Without that code hack, the problem has never been observed during
631: development and testing.
632: 
633: UPDATE: 2026-08-24 → Phil Eaton has devised
634: a reproducer that does not involve using the special testing code hack.
635: See Another look at SQLite's WAL-Reset bug
636: for details.
637: 
638: This bug, though rare, does have serious consequences, and so
639: application developers should upgrade to a version of SQLite
640: that fixes the problem.
641: However, this is not an emergency.
642: Based on available telemetry, the occurrence rate of this problem in the
643: wild appears to be less than or equal to the expected occurrence rate of
644: SSD malfunctions and/or cosmic-ray hits. So even if you are running an
645: unpatched version of SQLite, and unless you are doing something really
646: unusual, you are unlikely to ever encounter this problem.
